Subject: Dedicated capacity question — burst windows and pre-warm

Hi Kimberly / Vivek,

Thanks for the demo last week. We liked the latency profiles on the hosted side and want to explore Redwood Dedicated for our production inference (customer-facing assistant). Before we engage procurement, we need to understand how you handle short, high-intensity "burst" traffic on Dedicated pools. A few concrete asks: 

- If we sign a 3-node reserved pool (A100-equivalent), what headroom do you recommend to safely absorb 10x traffic spikes that last 30–90 minutes?
- Is there a pre-warm or standby slab option so warm-start latency stays within 300ms p95?
- How does autoscaling interact with per-deal committed capacity (eviction/priority rules)?
- Any thoughts on cost for transient burst capacity billed separately vs. upfront reserved buffer?

We can share typical hourly qps and token distribution if that helps sizing. Attaching a short traffic sample.

Cheers,
Lena

TerraScale

From: kimberly_park@redwood.ai

Subject: Re: Dedicated capacity question — burst windows and pre-warm

Lena — thanks for the sample. Copying Dev and Vivek to scope the technical options. High level answers up front:

- We recommend a committed baseline sized to meet 95% of your steady-state token/sec demand, plus a reserved burst pool for short windows. For a 3-node baseline we typically recommend 30–50% additional "buffer" capacity for 30–60 min spikes; for 10x spikes a short-lived pre-warm + burst slab is better than permanently oversizing.
- Pre-warm: we can keep a warm standby slab (hot caches + warmed KV) behind your Dedicated account for a predictable per-minute cold-start budget. This reduces p95 to target SLA levels.
- Autoscale behavior: requests are routed to committed capacity first; burst pool capacity is used when baseline is saturated. We offer priority rules so critical endpoints keep precedence and non-critical jobs can be overflowed or queued. Eviction only occurs when we reach regional limits and is governed by the SLA tier + the deal's priority tag.
- Billing: burst is metered by minute/token at a higher rate than reserved capacity; for large customers we can negotiate tranche pricing or credits.

Dev — see Lena's sample attached. Can you draft a quick sizing note and an example burst policy (pre-warm size, warm-up time, eviction priority) we can send to procurement? Vivek — we may need a short ops note on pre-warm maintenance and cache warming steps.

Thanks,
Kimberly Park
Account Executive, Redwood Inference

Subject: RE: Dedicated capacity question — Dedicated sizing note + burst policy draft

Hi all — I put together a concise sizing sketch based on the CSV and a few assumptions. Summary below; full calc in attached workbook.

Assumptions (from sample): avg steady token/sec ~1,200, 95th ~2,400, peak short windows spike to ~12,000 tokens/sec (10x).

Sizing recommendation:
- Baseline committed pool: 4 A100-equivalent slots (covers steady+95th with 20% headroom)
- Burst slab: 2 additional nodes kept as "standby warm" for rapid absorption (targets 2–5 minute warm-up)
- Ephemeral scale: allow autoscale to add up to 6 transient nodes for extreme events, gated by autoscale policy and regional capacity.

Burst policy (draft):
1) Pre-warm slab: 2 nodes with warmed KV/cache maintained at all times during business hours — billed as "standby burst" at agreed discounted rate.
2) Automatic short-burst fill: if CPU/GPU queue latency > 40ms and baseline is saturated, route to pre-warm slab. If pre-warm is saturated, initiate ephemeral node provisioning (up to 6 nodes).
3) Eviction/priority: Mark TerraScale endpoints as "gold" priority; ephemeral nodes evict non-gold tenants first if regional capacity exhausted.
4) Graceful degradation: non-critical jobs (batch/reranking) are rate-limited first. Chat/generation endpoints keep lower concurrency but preserved memory state.

Operational notes:
- Warm-up time: with cached KV we see 90% of steady-state throughput in ~90s; with pre-warm that drops to ~10–20s for p95 latency catch-up.
- Cache warming: we run a lightweight prefetch of top N prompts and prefix cache during pre-warm to minimize latency cliffs.
- Observability: we will provide route-level token/latency charts and auto-alerts for burst events.

I've attached the workbook with per-hour sims. If this aligns, I'll convert to a one-page for procurement and add concrete billing examples.

Thanks,
Dev Patel
Senior Systems Engineer, Redwood Inference

[Attachment: terra_capacity_estimate_v1.xlsx (Excel workbook, 52KB)]

Subject: RE: Dedicated capacity question — cost example + hybrid routing note

Lena, Kimberly — attaching the draft cost example and a short note on hybrid routing. Highlights:

- Cost (sample month): baseline 4-node committed pool + 2-node pre-warm (business hours) + ephemeral minutes for events described = estimated $64,800/mo. This includes a 15% enterprise discount tied to TS-2026-089. Spreadsheet attached.
- Billing model: pre-warm billed as reserved "standby" line item; ephemeral billed per-minute with a cap and surge discount tiers (we can commit a monthly cap in contract).
- Hybrid routing: supported via Private deployment peering. We can register customer-managed ephemeral instances as compatible targets; Redwood control plane will route to those nodes if they present the agreed runtime fingerprint and are healthy. Networking/peering and security review required.

Next steps: Kimberly, if TerraScale accepts the sizing and cost approach we can push a short SOW addendum describing the standby slab, surge caps, and the hybrid routing checklist. I'll attach the draft SOW and the cost workbook.

Best regards,
Evelyn Hart
VP, Customer Success — Redwood Inference
